This 1969 Chevy Impala Hasn't Moved an Inch in 10 Years, Big-Block Surprise Under the Hood
28 photos
Photo: eBay seller ccca_305
This 1969 Chevrolet Impala hasn’t moved a single inch in the last 10 years. The reason wasn’t shared on eBay, where the owner decided to list the car, but the Impala is now ready to get back into action and return to the road.
The car looks like an easy project, as the issues you can spot in these photos don’t suggest anything that could become a reason to walk away.
Sure, it also depends on your expectations. If you’re particularly interested in an all-original Impala, you’ll have to inspect this car in person because it’s unclear if this is the case. But if you just want a regular driver that you can take out on sunny Sundays, this Impala seems to be a good choice.
Photo: eBay seller ccca_305 Born in 1958 as a Bel Air version and promoted to a stand-alone series a year later, the Impala rapidly became the best-selling Chevrolet. It continued to dominate the brand’s sales throughout the next decade, and the 1969 model year made no difference.
The Impala was still the top full-size Chevrolet , accounting for 777,000 cars of all 1.1 million full-size units built by the GM brand. The Caprice was the runner-up, but the difference was huge: only 166,000 buyers ordered a Caprice. The Bel Air fell to a little over 155,000 cars, while the Biscayne, which continued to be the most affordable full-size Chevrolet, represented only 68,700 orders.
One of the biggest changes that happened in the Impala lineup in 1969 was how Chevrolet offered the Super Sport. No longer being offered as an option or separate series, the Super Sport could only be ordered as part of the Z24 package, which represented the SS 427, available only for the Sport Coupe, the Custom Coupe, and the convertible.
Fitted with a 427ci engine rated at 390 horsepower, the Super Sport could be had for no more, no less than $422.
This wasn’t the most powerful engine in the lineup, though. While Chevrolet continued to offer a six and a 327 as the base engines, the company also wanted to offer as much power as possible for those who wanted to get a boost of adrenaline behind the wheel of an Impala. In addition to the L36, which could also be ordered without the SS treatment for $237, buyers could also get the L72.
This was an upgraded version of the 427, this time rated at 425 horsepower and carrying an extra price (for non-SS buyers) of $447.
Photo: eBay seller ccca_305 This Impala is fitted with the non-SS 427 rated at 335 horsepower, and according to the seller, it still runs great. This is certainly good news, considering the car has been off the road for a while, so my recommendation is that you still ask your mechanic to inspect it in person before you make an offer.
There are things that don’t work on this car, so the time in storage has clearly taken its toll. The hideaway headlights aren’t working despite still being complete.
However, the vehicle is still very solid, at least based on the photos published online. There’s obvious corrosion, but I don’t think this is a critical problem. The images don’t reveal any rot or rust that has gotten through, so the damage is mostly on the surface and should be easy to deal with.
The best thing about this car is that it’s still complete, so even if something is not in its best shape, it should be fixable. Sure, nobody can tell this for sure unless they see the car live, so call the seller and maybe ask for a digital walkaround to see the advertised solid floors and trunk more thoroughly.
Photo: eBay seller ccca_305 The price isn’t necessarily surprising, considering this is a big-block 1969 Chevrolet Impala. An SS would have made it significantly more appealing to full-size Chevrolet fanboys, but at first glance, it still checks many of the right boxes to get a full refresh.
There are questions left without an answer, including regarding the car’s originality. A demanding collector or die-hard Chevy fan would look for the full package, so more information is certainly required for this Impala.
The seller listed the car for auction, with the starting bid set at $28,000. A reserve is also in place, but that’s not necessarily bad news because it’s unlikely to be far from the Buy It Now price, which has been configured at $36,400. This is the price anyone has to pay to get their hands on the car without a fight, though right now, the auction is still at zero bids.
The digital fight should come to an end in 8 days, but if nobody submits an offer, we should see this Impala getting relisted in the coming weeks. The car is parked in East Meadow, New York, and it should be able to move on its own power after it sells.
